headline: US military uses high-energy lasers to shoot down three Mexican cartel drones over southern border
summary: The uncrewed aerial vehicles were destroyed by an "Army Multipurpose High Energy Laser System" and were suspected of being used for surveillance and human smuggling.
details: The U.S. military recently shot down three drones suspected of operating for Mexican cartels. These uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAVs) were destroyed by an "Army Multipurpose High Energy Laser System" operated by U.S. Northern Command (USNORTHCOM) between Tuesday evening and Wednesday morning.

Maj. Gen. Curtis Taylor, commander of the southern border's Joint Task Force, stated that cartel networks are increasingly employing UAVs to facilitate illicit human-smuggling and actively spy on personnel. He emphasized that such hostile surveillance will not be tolerated, integrating layered countermeasures with advanced directed-energy capabilities.

It remains unclear whether the drones were shot down over American or Mexican airspace, though a military spokesperson confirmed actions were taken in coordination with all partners along the border. This incident follows previous uses of laser weapons, including one that mistakenly targeted party balloons and another that hit a Customs and Border Protection unit drone.

The military has declined to release further details on the recent shoot-downs, citing operational security and ongoing operations. The deployment of anti-drone laser systems is a growing trend, with the UK planning to equip Royal Navy destroyers by 2027 and China developing man-portable systems.

While expensive to acquire, laser defense systems are significantly cheaper to operate than traditional man-portable air defense systems (MANPADS), with each shot costing as little as $13. This economic feasibility makes them increasingly viable for defending against drones, a tactic notably highlighted by their effective use in Ukraine.

headline_marked: [[Arbitrary code execution in QubesOS]] via copy-to-VM error reporting backchannel
headline: Arbitrary code execution in QubesOS via copy-to-VM error reporting backchannel
summary: Qubes Security Bulletin (QSB) 118 details a critical vulnerability allowing arbitrary code execution in Dom0. This flaw is exploited through the qvm-copy-to-vm error reporting mechanism.
details: Qubes Security Bulletin (QSB) 118 has been published, addressing a critical vulnerability that allows arbitrary code execution in Dom0. This flaw is specifically found within the qvm-copy-to-vm error reporting backchannel. Users are urged to update their systems.

QSBs are official security announcements from the Qubes security team, providing summaries and impact analyses of recently discovered software vulnerabilities. They also detail the necessary patching instructions to mitigate risks.
While most vulnerabilities are addressed by normal system updates, some cases may require special user actions. The QSB outlines all required steps to protect against the identified security flaws.

The Qubes security team cryptographically signs all QSBs with PGP signatures, allowing users to verify their authenticity. This prevents forged bulletins from deceiving users into actions that could compromise their system's security.

Verifying the PGP signatures is crucial to ensure the QSB is genuine, protecting against potential malware installations or configuration changes that could leave the system vulnerable. Users should authenticate the Qubes Master Signing Key (QMSK) out-of-band.
